across hierarchical tasks, we adopt task-specific metrics tailored to each prediction objective. For semantic segmentation, we use mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU), a standard metric that accounts for pixel-wise accuracy under class imbalance. For each class  $ k \in \{1, \ldots, K-1\} $, the IoU is defined as
$$ \mathrm{IoU}_{k}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}_{k}}{\mathrm{TP}_{k}+\mathrm{FP}_{k}+\mathrm{FN}_{k}} $$
where  $ TP_{k} $,  $ FP_{k} $, and  $ FN_{k} $ denote true positives, false positives, and false negatives for class k, respectively. The mIoU is then computed as the average across classes:
$$ \mathrm{mIoU}=\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\mathrm{IoU}_{k}. $$
This metric evaluates the model's ability to accurately delineate fine-grained anatomical regions, which are critical for downstream tasks.

For morphological trait prediction, given its multi-label binary nature, we adopt the macro-averaged F1-score to balance precision and recall across traits. For each trait  $ j \in \{1, \ldots, T\} $, precision and recall are determined as follows
$$  Precision_{j}=\frac{TP_{j}}{TP_{j}+FP_{j}} $$
$$ \mathrm{Recall}_{j}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}_{j}}{\mathrm{TP}_{j}+\mathrm{FN}_{j}} $$
and the corresponding F1-score is given by:
$$ \mathrm{F1}_{j}=\frac{2\cdot\mathrm{Precision}_{j}\cdot\mathrm{Recall}_{j}}{\mathrm{Precision}_{j}+\mathrm{Recall}_{j}}. $$
In addition, we employ mean Average Precision (mAP) to evaluate ranking performance across traits. The Average Precision (AP) for each trait j is defined as:
$$ \mathbf{A}\mathbf{P}_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{N}(R_{k}-R_{k-1})\cdot P_{k} $$
where  $ P_k $ and  $ R_k $ denote precision and recall at the  $ k $-th threshold when ranking samples by the predicted score  $ \hat{t}_j $,

and N is the number of samples. The mAP is then averaged over all traits
$$ \mathrm{mAP}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{j=1}^{T}\mathrm{AP}_{j}. $$
This metric complements the macro-F1 score by evaluating the model's ability to rank positive traits effectively.
For species classification, we use top-1 accuracy, which measures the proportion of correctly classified samples

$$ \mathbf{A}\mathbf{c}\mathbf{c}\mathbf{u}\mathbf{r}\mathbf{a}\mathbf{c}\mathbf{y}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(\underset{k}{\mathbf{a}}\underset{i,k}{\mathbf{g}}\mathbf{m a x}\hat{y}_{c,i,k}=y_{c,i}) $$

where N is the number of samples, and  $ \mathbb{I}(\cdot) $ is the indicator function. This straightforward metric evaluates the global categorization performance, benefiting from the hierarchical cues provided by lower-level tasks. Given the extreme class imbalance in Fish-Vista [1], we stratify performance into four frequency-based groups based on numbers of training samples: Majority ( $ \geq $ 500 images), Neutral (100 - 499), Minority (10 - 99), and Ultra-Rare (< 10). The Ultra-Rare metric is of particular interest as it reflects the model's ability to learn from few-shot examples.

Implementation details: Our framework is implemented in PyTorch. We utilize a Swin-Transformer Base (Swin-B) [33] pre-trained on ImageNet-22k as the shared backbone. The input images are resized to  $ 224 \times 224 $. We train for 50 epochs with a batch size of 32 on a single NVIDIA A5000 GPU using AdamW optimizer (learning rate  $ 1 \times 10^{-4} $, weight decay 0.01), including 5 epochs for the warm-up stage. To manage multi-task optimization, we use homoscedastic uncertainty weighting [14] to dynamically balance  $ L_c $,  $ L_t $, and  $ L_s $ as in Eq. (23).
